grains-of-paradise.name: Grains of paradise
grains-of-paradise.summary: A West African spice from a plant in the ginger family, related to cardamom, with a pungent, black-pepper-like flavor and hints of citrus.

xylopia-aethiopica.name: Grains of Selim
xylopia-aethiopica.summary: The dried fruit of an African rainforest tree, used as a spice and herbal medicine.

alligator-pepper.name: Alligator pepper
alligator-pepper.summary: West African spice made from the seeds and pods of certain ginger-family plants, related to grains of paradise, used for pungency and aroma in soups and stews.

monodora-myristica.name: Calabash nutmeg
monodora-myristica.summary: A tropical African tree, also called African nutmeg, whose seeds were once widely sold as a cheap substitute for true nutmeg.

portuguese-gold-coast.name: Portuguese Gold Coast
portuguese-gold-coast.summary: Portuguese colony on the coast of present-day Ghana, ruled from the São Jorge da Mina fortress founded in 1482. Gold was its main export, and it passed to the Dutch in 1642.

roselle-plant.name: Roselle
roselle-plant.summary: Flowering plant likely native to parts of Africa, spread to Asia and the West Indies in the 16th and early 17th centuries. Its stems yield fibre and its calyces are steeped to make a popular infusion.

ackee.name: Ackee
ackee.summary: Fruit native to tropical West Africa, long reputed to be poisonous but delicious when ripe and properly cooked. It is the national fruit of Jamaica and features in various Caribbean cuisines.

solanum-aethiopicum.name: Garden egg
solanum-aethiopicum.summary: Fruiting plant, also called the Ethiopian eggplant or bitter tomato, found in Asia and tropical Africa. Its ripe fruit looks like a cross between an eggplant and a tomato.

garri.name: Garri
garri.summary: West African flour, coarse to fine, made from starchy cassava root. Heating it removes natural toxins, and it is a staple food in Nigeria, Ghana, Benin and several neighbouring countries.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

malagueta-pepper.name: Malagueta pepper
malagueta-pepper.summary: Small, tapered chili, a variety of Capsicum frutescens, widely used in Portuguese-speaking countries and the Caribbean. It measures 60,000 to 100,000 Scoville units.

sonni-ali.name: Sonni Ali
sonni-ali.summary: The 15th ruler of the Sunni dynasty of the Songhai Empire, reigning about 1464 to 1492, who transformed it into an empire by conquering Timbuktu, Massina, the Inner Niger Delta and Djenne.

dyula-people.name: Dyula people
dyula-people.summary: Mande ethnic group of West Africa, in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Burkina Faso, known as successful merchants. From the fourteenth century they founded trading communities and helped Islam spread peacefully in the region.

jolof-empire.name: Jolof Empire
jolof-empire.summary: A Wolof state in what is now Senegal that ruled parts of Mauritania and Gambia from the mid-14th century until 1549.

thieboudienne.name: Thieboudienne
thieboudienne.summary: Traditional dish of Senegal, also eaten in Mauritania, Guinea, Mali, The Gambia and elsewhere in West Africa, and the country's national dish. It is made with fish, broken rice and tomato sauce cooked in one pot.

chevalier-des-marchais.name: Chevalier des Marchais
chevalier-des-marchais.summary: French cartographer, navigator and slave-ship captain (1674 to 1728) who traveled the west coast of Africa, the West Indies and northwest South America between 1704 and 1727. His maps and manuscripts were published after his death.

kola-nut.name: Kola nut
kola-nut.summary: Caffeine-containing seed of certain Cola trees native to Africa's tropical rainforests. Its use as a flavoring in soft drinks gave 'cola' its name.

akan-people.name: Akan people
akan-people.summary: A Kwa-speaking people of Ghana and Ivory Coast made up of subgroups such as the Asante and Fante, traditionally tracing royal descent through the mother's line.

elmina.name: Elmina
elmina.summary: A coastal town in Ghana that became the first European settlement in West Africa after the Portuguese built a fort there in the 1470s, growing into a major trading center.

shea-butter.name: Shea butter
shea-butter.summary: Fat taken from the nut of the African shea tree, ivory-coloured when raw. It is widely used in cosmetics as a moisturizer and is eaten in some African countries.

sankor-madrasah.name: Sankoré Madrasa
sankor-madrasah.summary: A medieval mosque and centre of learning in Timbuktu, founded in the 14th or early 15th century, where individual scholars taught private students rather than a formal university.

sudano-sahelian-architecture.name: Sudano-Sahelian architecture
sudano-sahelian-architecture.summary: An indigenous West African building style using mudbrick and adobe plaster with protruding wooden beams, seen in structures like the Great Mosque of Djenné.

bambara-people.name: Bamana people
bambara-people.summary: A Mandé ethnic group native to West Africa, mainly southern Mali, historically linked to the Bambara Empire and today the largest Mandé group in Mali.

s-gou-empire.name: Ségou (Bamana) Empire
s-gou-empire.summary: Also called the Bamana Empire, one of the largest West African states of the 18th century, growing from an earlier kingdom into a centralized empire under Bitòn Coulibaly from 1712 until conquered in 1861.

askia-al-hajj.name: Askia al-Hajj Muhammad
askia-al-hajj.summary: Ruler of the Songhai Empire from 1582 to 1586.

gao.name: Gao
gao.summary: A city in Mali on the River Niger, once a major trans-Saharan trade hub; it became capital of the Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali (1464–1492) after earlier being part of the Mali Empire.

osei-kofi-tutu-i.name: Osei Tutu I
osei-kofi-tutu-i.summary: Founder of the Asante Empire (c. 1660 to 1717) who, with priest Okomfo Anokye, united Asante states, defeated the regional power Denkyira in 1701, and built institutions of government that lasted nearly 200 years.

okomfo-anokye.name: Okomfo Anokye
okomfo-anokye.summary: The first priest of the Ashanti Empire, around 1655 to 1717, known for helping expand the empire and codifying its constitution and laws.

golden-stool.name: Golden Stool
golden-stool.summary: Sacred royal throne of the Asante people, said to have descended from the sky onto their first king, Osei Tutu, and believed to house the spirit of the Asante nation.

m-zab.name: M'zab
m-zab.summary: A natural region of the northern Sahara in Ghardaïa Province, Algeria, about 600 km south of Algiers, with roughly 360,000 inhabitants.

askia-ishaq-ii.name: Askia Ishaq II
askia-ishaq-ii.summary: Ruler of the Songhai Empire from 1588 to 1591 who commanded its forces at the Battle of Tondibi, where defeat by Saadian forces led to the empire's destruction.

saadi-sultanate.name: Saadi dynasty
saadi-sultanate.summary: An Arab Sharifian dynasty that ruled Morocco and parts of Northwest Africa in the 16th and 17th centuries, reaching its height under Ahmad al-Mansur.

judar-pasha.name: Judar Pasha
judar-pasha.summary: A Spanish-Maghrebi military leader, born Diego de Guevara and captured and castrated as a boy, who commanded the Saadian army that conquered the Songhai Empire in the late 16th century.

battle-of-tondibi.name: Battle of Tondibi
battle-of-tondibi.summary: The decisive battle of a 16th-century Moroccan invasion of the Songhai Empire, in which Moroccan forces under Judar Pasha defeated the Songhai under Askia Ishaq II, sealing the empire's downfall.

komenda-wars.name: Komenda Wars
komenda-wars.summary: A 1694-1700 series of wars in Ghana's Eguafo Kingdom between the Dutch and English trading companies over trade rights, drawing in African forces on both sides.

dutch-west-india-company.name: Dutch West India Company
dutch-west-india-company.summary: Dutch chartered company founded in 1621, given a monopoly on trade and colonisation across West Africa and the Americas, including a role in the Atlantic slave trade.

royal-african-company.name: Royal African Company
royal-african-company.summary: An English trading company established in 1660 with a monopoly on trade with Africa, which shipped more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other company before losing its monopoly in 1697.

eguafo.name: Eguafo
eguafo.summary: Guan kingdom in what is now southern Ghana, active from at least the 15th century, whose ports Shama and Elmina made it a major trading power until its 19th-century conquest by the Fante.

john-thornton-historian.name: John Thornton
john-thornton-historian.summary: American historian (born 1949) at Boston University specializing in African, African Diaspora and Atlantic World history.

bit-n-coulibaly.name: Bitòn Coulibaly
bit-n-coulibaly.summary: Founder of the Bambara Empire in what is now Mali's Ségou and Mopti regions, who lived roughly from 1689 to 1755.

s-gou.name: Ségou
s-gou.summary: A town in south-central Mali on the River Niger, about 235 km northeast of Bamako; it was capital of the Ségou Cercle and Ségou Region and Mali's fifth-largest town in 2009.

taghaza.name: Taghaza
taghaza.summary: An abandoned salt-mining centre in the Sahara in northern Mali, an important source of rock salt for trans-Saharan trade until it was abandoned at the end of the 16th century.

gajaaga.name: Gajaaga (Galam)
gajaaga.summary: A Soninke kingdom on the upper Senegal River, known as the Land of Gold for its gold exports, that existed from before 1000 CE until 1858 and was a vassal of Jolof and Takrur.

mahmud-iv-mansa.name: Mansa Mahmud IV
mahmud-iv-mansa.summary: Last reigning emperor of the Mali Empire according to a 17th-century chronicle; his 1599 defeat near Djenne ended Mali's imperial period, and his death split the empire among his sons.

niger-river.name: Niger River
niger-river.summary: The main river of West Africa, running about 4,180 kilometres in a crescent shape through southwest Mali before reaching the Atlantic Ocean; Africa's third-longest river.

begho.name: Begho
begho.summary: A trading city in what is now Ghana's Bono state, a cosmopolitan hub linking West and North African merchants before Europeans arrived in 1471.

tenguella.name: Tengela
tenguella.summary: Tenguella: A Fula chief who founded the short-lived Futa Kingui state in the upper Senegal River valley, a precursor to the Empire of Great Fulo. He himself was called the Great Fulo in Portuguese records of the time.

kong-empire.name: Kong Empire
kong-empire.summary: A pre-colonial West African trading state (1710-1898) centered on the city of Kong, built on merchant networks and Islamic scholarship until Samori Ture burned the city in 1898.

niani-guinea.name: Niani
niani-guinea.summary: A village in Guinea, in the Kankan Region, lying on the left bank of the Sankarani River.

djenn.name: Djenné
djenn.summary: Historic town in central Mali closely tied to Timbuktu through trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves, famed for its adobe Sudano-Sahelian architecture.

askia-daoud.name: Askia Daoud
askia-daoud.summary: Ruler of the Songhai Empire from 1549 to 1582, whose reign brought a peak of peace and prosperity after earlier succession disputes.

john-cabess.name: John Cabess
john-cabess.summary: African trader in Komenda, part of the Eguafo Kingdom in modern Ghana (c. 1640s–1722), a major British ally who became a leading economic and political force on the Gold Coast.

komenda-ghana.name: Komenda
komenda-ghana.summary: A town in Ghana's Central Region, split into British and Dutch sections linked by a bridge.

willem-bosman.name: Willem Bosman
willem-bosman.summary: Dutch merchant (1672–after 1703) for the Dutch West India Company on the Gold Coast, whose detailed 1704 account of the region became a major historical source.

panyarring.name: Panyarring
panyarring.summary: The 18th- and 19th-century West African practice of seizing people to force repayment of debts, later used to secure captives for the slave trade before being banned in the early 20th century.

mahmud-kati.name: Mahmud Kati
mahmud-kati.summary: An African Muslim Songhai scholar (1468?–1552 or 1593) traditionally credited as author of the West African chronicle Tarikh al-fattash, though this authorship is contested.

tarikh-al-fattash.name: Tarikh al-fattash
tarikh-al-fattash.summary: A West African chronicle covering the Songhai Empire from 1464 to 1599, later shown to combine an authentic 17th-century text with a 19th-century forgery falsely attributed to an earlier author.

leo-africanus.name: Leo Africanus
leo-africanus.summary: An Andalusi diplomat and author (c. 1494–c. 1554) best known for his 1526 work on the geography of the Maghreb and Nile Valley, later published as Description of Africa and long considered Europe's most authoritative treatise on the region.

tarikh-al-sudan.name: Tarikh al-Sudan
tarikh-al-sudan.summary: A West African chronicle written in Arabic around 1655 by a Timbuktu scholar, considered the single most important primary source for the history of the Songhai Empire.

mero.name: Meroë
mero.summary: An ancient city on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kush from around 590 BC until its collapse in the 4th century AD.

sekondi-takoradi.name: Takoradi
sekondi-takoradi.summary: One of the twin cities in Ghana that grew from 17th-century Dutch and English trading forts and merged with Sekondi in 1946.

ahanta-people.name: Ahanta people
ahanta-people.summary: An Akan people from what is now Ghana's Western Region, historically a wealthy coastal confederacy of chiefdoms that traded early with European nations on the Gold Coast.

fetu-kingdom.name: Fetu Kingdom
fetu-kingdom.summary: A Guan-Akan state on Ghana's coast near Cape Coast from the 15th century, a key broker in early Atlantic trade before being absorbed into the Fante Confederacy by the mid-17th century.

andr-thevet.name: André Thevet
andr-thevet.summary: French Franciscan priest, explorer, cosmographer and writer (1516-1590) who traveled to the Near East and South America and wrote a firsthand account of a French settlement near modern Rio de Janeiro.

shama-ghana.name: Shama, Ghana
shama-ghana.summary: A fishing town on Ghana's coast near the mouth of the Pra River, home to Fort San Sebastian, where philosopher Anton Wilhelm Amo is buried.

songhai-empire.name: Songhai Empire
songhai-empire.summary: A major West African state that flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries, eventually surpassing the Mali Empire in area, wealth and power under Sonni Ali and later the Askia dynasty.

faama.name: Faama
faama.summary: A Mandinka word for a martial ruler or king, used in pre-imperial Mali and later by the Bamana and Wassoulou empires, distinct from the more mystic royal title of mansa.

asante-empire.name: Asante Empire
asante-empire.summary: An Akan state in what is now Ghana that lasted from 1701 to 1902, known for its military strength, wealth, and trade in gold and other goods.

kingdom-of-denkyira.name: Kingdom of Denkyira
kingdom-of-denkyira.summary: A powerful Akan gold-producing kingdom in what is now Ghana that dominated neighboring states in the 17th century before its 1701 defeat and vassalage to the Asante Empire.

kurmina-fari.name: Kurmina-fari (kanfari)
kurmina-fari.summary: A major administrative and military title in the Songhai Empire, created in 1494 by Askia Mohammad I to govern the western half of the empire from Tindirma, often held by the ruler's brother or eldest son.

mansa-title.name: Mansa
mansa-title.summary: A Maninka and Mandinka word for a hereditary ruler, often translated as king or emperor, most famously as the title of rulers of the Mali Empire such as Mansa Musa.

sansanding.name: Sansanding
sansanding.summary: A small town in the Ségou Region of southern-central Mali on the Niger River, with about 23,000 residents as of 2009.

keita-dynasty.name: Keita dynasty
keita-dynasty.summary: The ruling Muslim dynasty of pre-imperial and imperial Mali from the 11th to early 17th century, claiming descent from Bilal ibn Rabah; its first mansa was Sundiata Keita.

mali-empire.name: Mali Empire
mali-empire.summary: A West African empire from about 1235 to 1610, founded by Sundiata Keita and renowned for the wealth of rulers like Mansa Musa; at its peak the largest empire in West Africa.

fouta-djallon.name: Futa Jallon
fouta-djallon.summary: A highland region in central Guinea, West Africa, that gave its name to a historic Fulani state governed from the capital Timbo.

ngolo-diarra.name: Ngolo Diarra
ngolo-diarra.summary: Faama (ruler) of the Bambara Empire from 1766 to 1790, a former slave warrior who seized the throne amid chaos after the empire's founder died and restored order and prosperity.

sultanate-of-massina.name: Sultanate of Massina
sultanate-of-massina.summary: State covering much of the Inner Niger Delta in present-day Mali, founded around 1400 and usually a tributary of larger empires until overthrown by jihad in 1818.

kangaba.name: Kangaba
kangaba.summary: A town in Mali believed founded in 1050, once a vassal of the Ghana Empire and later a core province of the Mali Empire, where Sundiata Keita proclaimed the Manden Charter in 1235.

aja-people.name: Aja people
aja-people.summary: An ethnic group native to southwestern Benin and southeastern Togo whose migrating branches helped form the Fon people; vodún is said to have originated with them.

fon-people.name: Fon people
fon-people.summary: Benin's largest ethnic group, historically called Dahomeans, who founded the Dahomey kingdom by the 17th century and speak Fongbe, a Gbe language of the Bight of Benin.

west-african-vod-n.name: Vodún
west-african-vod-n.summary: A West African traditional religion of the Aja, Ewe and Fon peoples teaching a supreme creator divinity ruling over lesser spirits called vodúns, with no central authority.

fula-people.name: Fula people
fula-people.summary: An ethnic group spread across the Sahara, Sahel and West Africa numbering 25 to 40 million; about a third are pastoralists, forming the world's largest nomadic pastoral community.

imamate-of-futa-jallon.name: Imamate of Futa Jallon
imamate-of-futa-jallon.summary: A West African Islamic state founded in 1725 by a Fulani jihad in the Fouta Djallon highlands of modern Guinea, becoming a leading religious centre before joining French West Africa in 1896.

usman-dan-fodio.name: Usman dan Fodio
usman-dan-fodio.summary: A Fulani Islamic scholar (1754–1817) who led a religious revolution in West Africa, founded the Sokoto Caliphate in 1803, and wrote over a hundred books on religion and society.

hausa-kingdoms.name: Hausa Kingdoms
hausa-kingdoms.summary: A collection of states ruled by the Hausa people in what is now northern Nigeria, situated between the western Sudanic empires and Kanem-Bornu before the Fulani jihads.

dahomey.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
dahomey.summary: A West African kingdom in present-day Benin, existing from about 1600 to 1904, that grew powerful through conquest, the Atlantic slave trade, and an all-female military unit called the Dahomey Amazons.

oyo-empire.name: Oyo Empire
oyo-empire.summary: A Yoruba empire in what is now western Nigeria and Benin that became the largest Yoruba-speaking state and one of West Africa's most powerful states from the late 16th to early 18th century.

if-x.name: Ifá (Fá)
if-x.summary: A geomantic divination system originating among the Yoruba people of West Africa, overseen by the orisha Orunmila and practiced by initiates called babaláwo, which spread to other peoples and, through the slave trade, to the Americas.

egungun.name: Egungun
egungun.summary: Yoruba masquerade or masked figure for ancestor reverence, representing the spirits of the dead as they periodically revisit the living community.

tegbesu.name: Tegbesu
tegbesu.summary: King of the Kingdom of Dahomey, in present-day Benin, from 1740 to 1774, who took the throne after a succession struggle following his father Agaja's death.

karamokho-alfa.name: Karamokho Alfa
karamokho-alfa.summary: A Fula religious leader, born Ibrahima Musa Sambeghu, who led a jihad establishing the Imamate of Futa Jallon, the first Muslim state founded by the Fulbe, ruling until 1748 and dying around 1751.

almami.name: Almaamy
almami.summary: Title meaning "the leader," from the Arabic for imam, used by Tukulor monarchs and other West African Islamic theocratic rulers from the 1700s into the 1900s.

timbo-guinea.name: Timbo
timbo-guinea.summary: A town in the Fouta Djallon highlands of present-day Guinea, in an area mostly home to the Fula people.

sofa-warrior.name: Sofa
sofa-warrior.summary: A Mandinka term for slave soldiers who served in the army of the Mali Empire, and later in Mandé states such as the Bamana and Wassoulou empires.

mande-languages.name: Mandé languages
mande-languages.summary: A family of about 60 to 75 West African languages spoken by roughly 60 million people, including Mandinka, Bambara and Susu.

dinkoro-coulibaly.name: Dinkoro Coulibaly
dinkoro-coulibaly.summary: Ruler of the Bambara Empire from 1755 to 1757, relative of empire founder Bitòn Coulibaly, who soon lost control through military coups and was assassinated in 1757.

ali-coulibaly.name: Ali Coulibaly
ali-coulibaly.summary: King of the Bambara Empire of Ségou around 1757 to 1759, son of the empire's founder; a devout Muslim whose attempt to convert his subjects and ban on millet beer led to his overthrow.
